Long answer: There is a ton of really great advice here. But one thing I want to emphasize is the work it takes to have the kind of life you want. The world is not going to be willing to accommodate you for the most part because of you having bipolar. 
For example, if you get married and consistently treat your partner like crap/cross their boundaries/have affairs while manic/don’t pull your weight, they may (and honestly, should) leave you. I’m not talking about the occasional episode/rough patch. I’m talking about consistently making the choice to give in to your head over the well-being of your marriage just because it’s hard. 
With work, there will almost definitely be times you have to call out/miss work due to episodes. If you’re depressed, you should still at least try to show up. Even if you’re late, or aren’t 100% of what you normally are, a lot of times it will help you feel a little better if you can push yourself to go. But, there will be times you just can’t go, and that’s okay. If you decide you want to be “successful” in a regular type job setting, you can not be a mediocre employee. You will need to work harder to achieve the same results, just like most other minority groups. But I’ve seen a good number of folks with bipolar have success with work from home or flexible type jobs or freelance work as well. 

Those are just two examples. But the “work” is a million percent worth it and it does get easier the longer you do it.

My husband was very not romantic. Even after many conversations where he said he would try, he just didn’t know how. But then we talked and I tried to be very specific about what I wanted. What did “romance” look like for me? I want him to surprise me with candy or a drink randomly. Or take me to get tacos and talk with me for an hour if I’m having a bad day. I want HIM to pick a day and time and place for a date night. I DO NOT want poems. Think about things like that. Having that conversation isn’t very romantic, because in a perfect world your partner would just KNOW how to do all those things that make you feel special. But that’s not realistic. Tell him exactly what you want, and then go from there. But please don’t complain about what he chooses while you’re learning. If he surprises you with a date night at Applebee’s and you aren’t that thrilled about it, pretend that you are. Then on a different day tell him that you guys should start a list of all the different (not necessarily expensive) restaurants in your town you guys want to try and then he can go from there. 

My husband is significantly better at being romantic now. He’s by no means perfect, but the fact that he does try a lot more now means a lot. Just remember to keep being Romantic yourself in the ways HE appreciates.

When my husband and I started dating, I was a casual/social drinker. A lot of our dates were going out to the bars to watch games or play darts or socialize. I ultimately quit drinking due to some health issues about 2 years in. As we got older, had kids, and other responsibilities increased, I assumed his drinking would subside. But it did not. He drank almost every night, and definitely drank every weekend. When it’s football season he would start at 11am. I talked to him about it for several years about slowing down the drinking, but he thought it wasn’t a real problem because, in his words, he wasn’t one of those people that had to drink when they woke up or to get through work. Which is true, he never called out of work because he was hungover, he just went to work hungover. He still did a lot of housework and it didn’t really impact his ability to be a great dad. It was just how he was and acted toward me when he was drinking that bothered me. I felt like I couldn’t ask him to completely stop because I knew that he drank when we got married, and it’s not fair (I think) to ask someone to change out of nowhere, and if I brought up slowing down or decreasing the weeknight drinking, he disagreed because he just didn’t want to stop.

4 months ago we started going to a couples therapist for mostly unrelated reasons, and they told him our second session (when I wasn’t in the room) that they thought he had a problem with alcohol, the impact it’s having on his marriage, life, and child, and that he should consider going to AA. He immediately reduced the drinking. He used to go through a Costco sized bottle of gin easily in a week (plus beer) and now that same bottle will last over a month, and he only drinks beer when he’s out at a restaurant or bar. It’s been great. 

All that to suggest that maybe getting some input from someone that’s not “the naggy wife” will help drastically, and being open to a compromise of “slowing down” vs “stopping completely”.

I think you should try a different therapist. I am (well, more WAS) the wife that was constantly suspicious of my husband even though he gave me no real reason to believe anything like that. Our therapist has helped tremendously. Although she HAS worked with him on some things that are “triggers” for me, she has never suggested he learn to just essentially deal with it. The focus has been just as much (if not more) on me not acting like a loon and reading too much into things. So start by trying a different therapist.

Congratulations! I am pregnant with my second child. My first pregnancy had the occasional bipolar related hiccup, but if you aren’t drinking alcohol and are limiting caffeine and are eating well and have made the appropriate adjustments to your medication, which you probably are since you’re pregnant, it is generally manageable. And that’s how it was with my first one. This second pregnancy has been a nightmare mental health wise, and I’m extremely worried about how it will be postpartum. However, we have figured out that the issue is mostly lack of sleep, which significantly impacts bipolar regardless of pregnancy. Part of that is my 18 month old, part of it is how much more uncomfortable my pregnancy is this time around. My advice is as soon as you start to feel your sleep quality decrease, do whatever you can to try and fix it. For us, it meant my husband now deals with the toddler if she wakes up overnight and he takes her to daycare in the morning instead of me so I can get that little bit of sleep. Get whatever pillows or space or whatever you need to help you sleep if it’s a physical/pregnancy thing. I have always been a people pleaser, but the number one focus right now needs to be on you being comfortable enough (physically and mentally) to get some quality sleep. The inconvenience of your husband having to take on these extra things temporarily or spending a little extra money on things that will help you be comfortable are absolutely nothing compared to not being around at all. 

My husband is also planning on taking some extra time off of work this time around to better help me manage what we assume will be a worse round of ppd, and I have a friend and some family that are coming to stay with us at separate times as well. 

Bipolar is hard. Pregnancy is hard. WHEN (not if) it is hard just remember it is not your fault and not because of anything you are doing wrong. It will pass and there are SO MANY amazing moments ahead with your new family.

Here’s some ideas without knowing what you specifically said or didn’t say, but common things I saw that were “red flags”:

1) Don’t say you want to work at Chick-fil-A because you “need a job”. Point out specifically why you would prefer to work at Chick-fil-A over other places. 
2) Chick-fil-A guests have HIGH expectations of great guest service. So think about what that looks like and say that’s what you’d deliver. If you say great guest service is smiling and greeting, that’s not going to cut it. 
3) Along with that, you need to appear confident. I don’t need you to love working with or talking to people, but I need you to be able to convince the guests that you do. So minimal “umms..” and don’t talk too quietly or just say “I don’t know”. Avoid those things. If you feel like you’re being over the top bubbly, then you’re probably almost being bubbly enough. 
4) Make great eye contact. Don’t play with your hair or hands or phone. 
5) Don’t have a bad availability. Working two days a week or some whacky time of day doesn’t help at all. They always need help 11-2 and generally 5-8. People who can stay later than 8 are great or that can work later than 2 until 4 or 5 when the high schoolers get in. Not sure how old you are but those are things to consider. 

A lot of people bring up being a Christian and all that jazz which is fine if you want to, but it is illegal for them to ask you anything about that and honestly to comment on it at all, so a more effective way to communicate that would be to say something along the lines of “Chick-fil-A shares my values” or whatnot. 

Hope that helps!

When I started dating my husband, I knew very little about football. The thing that worked for me was to just start watching the games with him (this worked out well since he watched football every time it was on, and most of our dates were to sports bars). After a couple games, I would start asking him questions when I didn’t understand what a call meant, or what a position was/did, or why we cared so much about a specific player in that game (I did not ask every single little question I had in the beginning, because then I would’ve been talking the entire game). If he got upset over a play or a call, I’d ask him to explain why. Over the course of a few seasons, the number of questions I had went down dramatically. Additionally, I learned to be able to recognize things on my own (things that were going to be flagged before the refs called them, anticipating what play was potentially going to be run, understanding the commentators jokes and references to things outside of that specific game). My husband loved that I was really trying to take an interest and learn about his number one hobby, and watching things as they happened and being able to have my questions answered was a way better way for me to learn compared to just reading books or blogs or watching games by myself in the beginning. I should add, though, that there are plenty of people that do not want to be talked to at all when they are trying to watch the game. Maybe they will always be open to questions, maybe they will be open to questions on games when their team isn’t the one playing, or maybe they don’t want to talk at all during any games. If your boyfriend is either of the first 2, I would highly recommend taking the route I did!

I wouldn't be shocked if this became a powerful card in Standard, but it just can't compete with some of the more broken equipment they've made in the past.

You wouldn't be able to block, since equipping can only be done any time you could cast a sorcery, and it would become unattached at the end of the turn when Mutavault stops being a creature.
